target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers and increase voting access for millions
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not reliably eliminate work-schedule barriers for many retail and service workers, because federal law does not require private employers to give paid holidays, so many hourly employees would still have to work.

target: AG1's implication that a holiday would broadly improve turnout
objection: An Election Day holiday by itself is not an effective strategy to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so it is unlikely to produce meaningful turnout gains on its own.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would not reliably remove scheduling barriers because some workers may still be required to work
objection: Even if a holiday does not eliminate every work barrier for every worker, a policy can still be justified if it meaningfully reduces the dominant schedule-based obstacle that keeps millions from voting.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday should be rejected because it does not fully solve work barriers and may not be the single best turnout reform
objection: Election-day policy should be judged on its democratic value and its ability to frame voting as a civic celebration, not only on whether it perfectly eliminates every work or school barrier or is the single most turnout-effective reform.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday is insufficient because it may not eliminate every work/school conflict
objection: The relevant question is whether the holiday meaningfully reduces the main scheduling barrier for millions of Americans, not whether it removes every barrier for every employee; reducing those conflicts would still increase access and participation.

target: AG2's suggestion that broad support and international precedent do not matter enough to justify the policy
objection: Because 71% of Democrats, 59% of Republicans, and many OECD countries support or use holiday/weekend elections, a national Election Day holiday is feasible, workable, and legitimately adopted rather than rejected merely because it is not perfect for every case.

target: AG2's view that only turnout-effectiveness matters
objection: Election Day policy should address both practical scheduling barriers and the civic-motivational benefit of treating voting as a celebration, so a holiday can be valuable even if it is not the only reform needed.

target: AG2's concern that a holiday could disadvantage low-income workers by leaving wage and scheduling obstacles in place
objection: Low-income hourly workers are exactly the people most harmed by election-day scheduling conflicts, so a holiday would reduce their time barrier and also elevate the civic value of voting rather than simply leaving them worse off.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would meaningfully reduce scheduling conflicts and increase turnout
objection: A national holiday would not reliably eliminate work/time barriers for many low-income hourly workers because private employers are not required to provide paid time off, so these workers could still lose wages or be unable to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would reduce administrative delays such as long waits at polling places
objection: Poll-worker shortages and long lines depend on recruitment, training, and operational staffing decisions, not on holiday status by itself, so a federal Election Day holiday would not reliably fix those delay problems.

target: AG1's reliance on international precedent to argue a holiday would work in the U.S.
objection: The fact that some countries hold elections on weekends or holidays does not show that a U.S. federal Election Day holiday would solve the wage-loss and paid-time-off barriers faced by low-income hourly workers, since U.S. private employers are not required to provide paid leave.
